newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. said tough in telecoms talks, EU gloomy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. said tough in telecoms talks, EU gloomy.

text.p: Trade diplomats said on Thursday the United States was taking a tough line in talks on a global pact to open up basic telecommunications, raising doubts an accord could be reached by the February 15 deadline.

And in Brussels European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan also struck a gloomy note, saying a deal was not yet done and suggesting the negotiations could, like a similar bid last year, still fail at the final hurdle.

U.S. officials in Geneva declined to give a detailed assessment of the state of play, but they said their team to the World Trade Organisation negotiations insisted better offers were still needed from other countries.
"The Americans are playing very hard," said one envoy. "It's beginning to look somewhat doubtful unless something gives somewhere."

"Right now, I would put the prospects at best at 50-50," said another key source close to the talks, billed as opening prospects for slashing the cost of phone calls in every corner of the globe by injecting competition into monopoly markets.

WTO envoys said strong pressure was being exerted by a U.S. team headed by Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang in bilateral talks for an improvement of market opening offers, especially on the degree of foreign ownership.
"I fear the U.S. is pushing the barrier very high," said one, adding: "It may be too high."

Success of the talks, the second effort in the last year to shape a WTO pact among some 60 countries accounting for over 91 percent of global telecommunications revenues totalling over $600 billion, depends entirely on the U.S. evaluation.

Diplomats say that as the largest single world telecommunications market, the United States is essential for a deal -- and could again walk away as it did last April just as other powers were saying agreement was within grasp.

On Wednesday, both the European Union and Canada expressed cautious optimism. But on Thursday Brittan, due in Geneva on Friday to try to push for a deal, called for all countries to "go that extra mile" to make it possible.

In a reference to the last effort, which collapsed when the United States walked away in April last year saying offers from other countries were not good enough, he said that experience was "a salutory reminder that negotiations can unravel even when they are on the brink of success."
Japan, another key player, was also less positive on Thursday over the outlook for a pact.

Akemi Yamaguchi, vice-minister for international affairs at Tokyo's Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, told reporters in Geneva "high quality" offers from some 60 countries were on the table which should be turned into a pact.
But he declined to give his own assessment of the prospects, and left no doubt Tokyo was among countries under strong pressure from Washington to improve aspects of its offer.

The United States argues that offers from other leading economies in both the developed and developing world have to be good enough to justify throwing open its lucrative home market to all comers, as it has offered.

The main focus of the U.S. drive appeared centred on getting key countries, especially Canada, to improve their offers of opening domestic telecoms companies to foreign ownership by pushing the allowed equity level above 50 per cent.
A senior Canadian official has said Ottawa's current offer of 47.8 percent cannot be changed, arguing that other aspects of his country's proposals made the package a very liberal one.

But diplomats close to the talks said increasing domestic pressure on the U.S. administration over trade issues might be making it harder for Washington to accept that line while offering a total opening of its own market.

One key U.S. senator is seeking to prevent Congressional approval of the nomination of Charlene Barshevsky as U.S. Trade Representative, a post she currently holds on an acting basis, by attaching conditions that could overshadow a telecom pact.
